Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to have this opportunity to speak on this most interesting bill both directly and indirectly, if hon. members will bear with me. First of all, I should like to indicate to the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) that I have read his bill with attention and think it is properly drafted. I might indicate, as well, that I agree with it in principle.
I find at this particular juncture in time that it is essential in the criminal process that there be adequate representation afforded an accused. In order to support my position I will not be referring to legal cases. Since being elected I have attempted to refrain from citing legal jurisprudence. I would, however, like to refer to a document I have found most interesting. It is entitled "Criminal Procedure Discovery" and is the fourth working paper of the Law Reform Commission of Canada. It is a document which in effect would support this particular bill as it indicates that in order to achieve a proper balance and equilibrium in our legal process, there has to be an equilibrium between the two antagonists, namely, the Crown on the one hand and the defence on the other.
Perhaps I might indicate, for members who are not thoroughly familiar with our criminal system of justice, that in fact we have what is referred to in Canada as an accusatorial or adversary system. It is to be compared to
June 10, 1975

the inquisitorial system used in France and Germany. Basically, in Canada it has always been recognized that our criminal system of justice is one which seeks to establish the guilt or innocence of the party brought before the court. In order to achieve that particular end, it was felt that we had to pursue the truth. In the pursuit of the truth there were a number of barriers placed in the way. Those barriers were placed there because we felt that in the pursuit of the truth we were running the danger of creating some injustices. Let me refer to a citation from this working paper, namely, the statement of Vice-Chancellor Knight Bruce in the case of Pearse v. Pearse (1846). ViceChancellor Knight Bruce said:
Truth, like all the good things, may be loved unwisely-may be pursued too keenly-may cost too much.
In effect, it is clear, as cited in that particular case, that society is not prepared, in its search for truth, to trample on the right to human dignity and privacy. The first concern we have is that when we are trying to establish guilt or innocence we do not trample upon privacy or human dignity. It seems to me that my friend's bill comes within that particular domain. The other concern we have is that we ought not to convict an innocent person while attempting to establish guilt. That has always been recognized. I shall paraphrase an old saying which I am sure has been misquoted on a number of occasions. It is to the effect that it is better that ten guilty persons should be freed than that one innocent person should be convicted. I fully agree with that.
In order to implement particular barriers and implement the pursuit of truth, we have brought into our criminal justice the adversary system. We could, as did the French and Germans, have adopted the system of inquisition where the judge is the one who conducts the investigation. In that system the whole investigation is conducted before a judicial officer and guilt or innocence is established.
However, because of the unfortunate experience with relation to the Star Chamber in the United Kingdom, in the mother of parliaments and the mother of our administrations, we felt it was important, especially after the experiences of the Spanish inquisitorial period, that we ought not to opt for inquisition as the method of establishing guilt or innocence but, instead, should move toward the adversary system. I suppose we based our choice on the system used by the knights, who in order to determine guilt or innocence fought each other and the winner was judged to be the innocent party. We have transferred that system to our criminal courts where on the one hand the Crown prosecutor represents the state and proceeds to bring the criminal to justice and attempts to persuade the court that the individual is guilty, while on the other hand we have the defence, namely the accused, who resists the accusation of the prosecutor and seeks to have the case against him diminished.
As an assistance to the accused we have given him the presumption that he is innocent until proven guilty. In that particular context, in the pursuit of truth we have managed-I suggest this very sincerely-to respect human dignity and to protect to a certain extent against unnecessary conviction. It has been suggested that sometimes
Canada Evidence Act
there is public pressure to secure convictions and that when we succumb to that particular pressure the unnecessary conviction of innocents results.
It is in that context I find this bill is timely, because we have now reached a level of sophistication in our investigation of crime. We have created a number of statutes to which Canadian subjects are subjected, if I might use the term twice in one sentence. In effect, it is very difficult for the citizen of Canada to know exactly what action he has committed and how that action could in some way infringe a criminal or quasi-criminal statute either at the federal or provincial level. It is, therefore, essential in this complex society that before an individual performs any action which may be detrimental to his defence before the tribunals, he receives full assistance from legal counsel.
I was fortunate to have practised at the criminal bar for nearly seven years before I became a member of parliament. I must admit that of all the facets of my practice at that time, that was the most interesting and most stimulating. I had occasion, as well, to act as duty counsel under the Ontario duty counsel or legal aid plan. I acted in that capacity in smaller communities of northern Ontario, having gone there from Toronto where I had practised for four years. In these communities I was amazed at the absence of information made available to an accused, not because of any intention to deprive the accused of his rights but simply because there was not a tendency among the constabulary or the prosecuting attorney to furnish an accused with that sort of information which would be beneficial. I therefore found that perhaps I could be of assistance in that regard.
It was with a great deal of pleasure that I found the legal aid plan in the province of Ontario was of tremendous assistance in this regard. I was very pleased, therefore, when I became a member of parliament, to find that the government of which I am a supporter was furnishing substantial sums to the individual provinces in order to permit them to implement their own provincial legal aid plans.
When I say this legislation is timely, I do so because we are now at a stage when legal assistance is available to Canadians from coast to coast. I note with some interest that the hon. member for Winnipeg North has recognized this. I am sure he was mindful of this when he proposed his bill, because in the new section 56 we find this provision:
If, pursuant to section 54 a request for counsel is made, the person in authority shall give the person who made the request an opportunity to contact his counsel or advise the local legal aid office director in the event the person who made the request cannot afford counsel.
I feel any provincial legal aid plan should have the obligation of making counsel available at any time this is required. I say that is so because of the fact that unless there is some mandatory requirement it may be very difficult for the police to continue their investigation as a result of there not being any lawyer available to advise the person accused. We could well find ourselves in a situation where an individual is arrested under suspicious circumstances, brought before the authorities in order to permit them to continue their investigation, and then if this bill were accepted the person would be advised that he has the right to obtain counsel, at which time the police

June 10, 1975
Canada Evidence Act
would have to wait until counsel was retained for that individual.

By that time, Mr. Speaker, that pattern of malfeasance might have disappeared. The opportunity for the Crown to complete its investigations would in fact be almost ruined and, of course, there would be no justice.
It is necessary however to achieve a balance. An officer of the court should be appointed by the province to meet the needs of the accused and inform him of his rights.
At the outset of my speech, Mr. Speaker, I referred to the working paper of the Law Reform Commission entitled "Criminal Procedure Discovery". Obviously, this document proves that there is an imbalance in the present procedure because the police and the Crown have all the authority and the means required to conduct their investigations and obtain the essential evidence. And in obtaining this evidence, some aspects of it that could be beneficial to the accused are not disclosed to him. Of course, his counsel cannot establish what is this evidence because the Crown never produces it. Such are the provisions of the Evidence Act at present. The accused has no way of finding out what aspects of the investigation or what facts revealed by the investigation of the Crown could be of assistance to him. Then, this document mentions that there should be a process of discovery of evidence to allow the defence to know what the situation is. Of course, this would eliminate to a certain extent the difficulties now experienced by the accused.
Mr. Speaker, you know that the accused has often said too much before assistance can be provided. Then, it is hard for him as well as for his lawyer to find out the true facts that could help him. I remember defending on many occasions accused people who had been intimidated by the police to such an extent that they could not relate to me what had happened before their arrest. They had forgotten certain facts which could have been essential to their defence. Naturally, the police, who were aware of those facts, refused to reveal them.

So, Mr. Speaker, I would suggest that the passage of this bill would perhaps permit even to a greater extent the bringing to fruition of the recommendations made in working paper No. 4 on criminal procedure of the Law Reform Commission of Canada, namely, discovery, because there is no doubt that since there are a greater number of lawyers involved in criminal law there is greater pressure on the authorities who administer justice to change the rules effectively so that if we are to maintain an adversary system that is fair to all parties, the accused as well as the Crown, they should be somewhat equal before the courts when they present their cases. In effect, by having more solicitors directly involved in the system of criminal justice, we may best achieve this.
If I might just reiterate, in summary the point is that we have an adversary system, and that is a system where there is a prosecutor and a defence. The judge sits passively and determines guilt or innocence. It is based upon the belief that by both the prosecution and the defence showing their mettle and arguing their own cases to the best of

their ability, all forces being equal, the truth will emerge, mindful of all those pxOsections the law of evidence has furnished.
However, in such a contest between the prosecution and the defence it is impossible to arrive at a just decision unless there is an equilibrium between the two forces. If the defence is not represented by counsel, or if at one time in the legal process the defence was not represented by counsel, it is impossible to establish that equilibrium. I say that contest begins immediately upon the arrest of the individual who is suspected. He ought to be advised as to what his rights are, just as the police or the investigators are advised as to their particular rights as peace officers or public authorities.
In conclusion, if we can achieve that with this bill, I will support it, and I have no doubt that we will achieve that particular equilibrium with this bill. Hopefully as an offshoot we will find ourselves with a new system of discovery, so that effectively our system of justice will do what it is intended to do. It is intended to find the truth after due pursuit, with all respect to human dignity and the right of the individual.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ASSURE PERSON'S RIGHTS CONSIDERED WHEN MAKING INCRIMINATING STATEMENT TO POLICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened with interest to the speeches of the hon. members who spoke before me and I admired the style and the political thinking of my colleague, the member for Nipissing (Mr. Blais) who has been able to inform us of his vast experience in the criminal field and of his personal and professional findings on the subject now before us.
As for me, I am always a little surprised at the way our parliamentary system works where some subjects can be so important; whereas in other countries, these subjects to be found in constitutions or in bills of rights; while we find them in a statute under a title as dull inocuous and common as an Act to amend the Canada Evidence Act (incriminating statements).
When I was practising law, although I never had the opportunity to practice criminal law, as did my colleague, the hon. member for Nipissing-unfortunately, neither my clients, my friends nor even some of my acquaintances were involved in that field. Most of the people who came to consult me belonged to the other side. With regard to the Evidence Act, Mr. Speaker, we remember quite well that, in French-speaking Law schools we were told by our professors that they did not want to lecture on evidence. It goes without saying that the obvious does not require long speeches.
However, the matter raised by the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) is serious and important. A quick glance at the bill reveals that it is extremely difficult to find fault with or to object to the kind of representations being made by the hon. member. Whoever is interested in our civil law and I am one of them, may be impressed by the added protection the hon. member would like to see in our Canadian law.
However, Mr. Speaker, as was suggested by the hon. member for Nipissing, the need to strike a balance, to reach a suitable compromise, is always present is these matters.
June 10, 1975

We must protect the rights of the individual, but we should also protect the rights of society, the people, who are also entitled to some protection. In these matters, I suggest we should always consider both sides.
When I read the bill, I am amazed at the fact that no reference was made to one particular provision which is included in clause 58, the last clause in Bill C-233.
No statement shall be admissible in evidence against its author in any criminal proceeding if he was without the benefit of counsel at the time the statement was made, unless the author knowingly and voluntarily waived his right to counsel.
Although much of the bill is, in effect, a codification of the protection normally afforded by our jurisprudence to the accused who makes a voluntary statement under our present legal system, I suggest that this provision is not a codification of current practice.
I suggest this is rather an extension of current practice, because the bill is affecting the admissibility of evidence. I have already referred to this matter in this House. I have great difficulty seeing this extension in connection with this subject because in my opinion, it would prevent the court from pursuing its quest for truth and would leave out evidence that may not have come up in the best circumstances, but which may still allow the court to clearly understand a case. Personally, I have always objected and will always object to the fact that a man who has committed a crime may escape conviction because the evidence against him might have been obtained illegally.
After all, as the hon. member has said, the American way of thinking which is being adopted goes much further than that based on the jurisprudential traditions of Canada and England. Like the hon. member who has introduced this bill, I read last night the rather exceptional judgment rendered in the case Miranda v. Arizona. In this case, I was struck by certain views aired by Chief Justice Warren, for instance, when he made an historical review of the way the principles involved in this bill were adopted in the United States and also in England. I hope you will excuse my accent when I quote Latin expressions. I would like to read a short extract from this judgment. On page 705 of the 1966 issue of the U.S. Report, the Chief Justice said, and I quote:
Over 70 years ago, our predecessors on this court eloquently stated: "The maxim nemo tenetur seipsum accusare had its origin in a protest against the inquisitorial and manifestly unjust methods of interrogating accused persons, which (have) long obtained in the continental system, and, until the expulsion of the Stuarts from the British throne in 1688, and the erection of additional barriers for the protection of the people against the exercise of arbitrary power, (were) not uncommon even in England. While the admissions or confessions of the prisoner, when voluntarily and freely made, have always ranked high in the scale of incriminating evidence, if an accused person be asked to explain his apparent connection with a crime under investigation, the ease with which the questions put to him may assume an inquisitorial character, the temptation to press the witness unduly, to browbeat him if he be timid or reluctant, to push him into a corner, and to entrap him into fatal contradictions, which is so painfully evident in many of the earlier state trials, notably in those of Sir Nicholas Throckmorton, and Udal, the Puritan minister, made the system so odious as to give rise to a demand for its total abolition. The change in the English criminal procedure in that particular seems to be founded upon no statute and no judicial opinion, but upon a general and silent acquiescence of the courts in a
Canada Evidence Act
popular demand. But, however adopted, it has become firmly embedded in English, as well as in American jurisprudence. So deeply did the iniquities of the ancient system impress themselves upon the minds of the American colonists that the States, with one accord, made a denial of the right to question an accused person a part of their fundamental law, so that a maxim, which in England was a mere rule of evidence, became clothed in this country with the impregnability of a constitutional enactment."

Mr. Speaker, this accounts for one of the basic differences between the jurisprudential traditions of the United States, which adopted the 5th Amendment, and our own jurisprudential evolution following the judgments referred to by the Chief Justice of the Supreme Court of the U.S. and which have resulted simply in a consolidation of section 5 of the Canada Evidence Act rather than in a constitutional provision.
Once again, Mr. Speaker, I object to that part of the bill which deals with the acceptability or exclusion of illegally obtained evidence. This is provided for in the bill itself, and, frankly, I have several reservations on that. I was very happy this year to see that the Law Reform Commission, in its 10th volume on evidence entitled The Exclusion of Illegally Obtained Evidence, seems to share some of the concerns that I had myself voiced in this House when we discussed the acceptability of evidence obtained by means of wiretapping.
The Law Reform Commission is obviously an institution established by this Parliament, a Commission which has been given specific terms of reference for reviewing in details all effects resulting from a change, especially in our Criminal Code. The Commission has also reviewed thoroughly other areas, but it was particularly responsible for the revamping and reform of our Criminal Code, and is, of course, now carrying out those terms of reference.
A number of reports have been tabled by the Commission, one of which is Report No. 10 which I referred to and which deals with the inadmissibility of evidence obtained illegally. I should like to quote from this report. As a matter of fact, the point is very well made at the outset of the document submitted to the Commission by the group reporting to the Commission. Here are two short paragraphs I should like to quote:

The question of whether illegally obtained evidence should be admissible has been debated at length, yet remains controversial. There are good arguments for what can be called the American position: the exclusion of both illegally obtained evidence and all other evidence derived from it. There are equally good arguments for the traditional English and Canadian positions: that evidence should not be excluded simply because it has been illegally obtained.

I am quoting now from the third paragraph:

It is often said that in criminal law, especially in matters of evidence, the legislator must find the proper balance between the imperatives of suppressing crime and guaranteeing fundamental human rights, between efficiency and fairness, between crime control and respect for individual freedom, and between the need to search for the whole truth and the need to safeguard certain basic values. The problem of admissibility of illegally obtained evidence raises these issues. Any solution to the problem reflects an inevitable choice between sets of apparently contradictory values.

June 10, 1975
Canada Evidence Act

Thereupon, the hon. member chose, as he could rightfully do, a solution truly designed to rule out evidence obtained illegally. This is not, however, the solution adopted by Parliament in various other cases.
I quoted a while ago the case of the Protection of Privacy Act, and if you refer to section 178, paragraph 16, of the Criminal Code, you will realize that Parliament had been made aware of this problem and had elected to allow the evidence obtained illegally. Although in a somewhat limited way.
There are also other cases. For instance, when a man is arrested for drunken driving, he must submit to a breath-alizer test. Of course, if the kind of principles the hon. member is talking about were to be expanded, I wonder why it should not cover also the breathalizer test, so that an individual could be told: "Of course, you are certainly not compelled to submit to a breathalizer test, unless you have a lawyer at your side".
Obviously, the application of an act whose effects have been most beneficial would become almost impossible. Inevitably, any person apprehended by the policy would then say: I cannot afford to retain a lawyer. Get me a legal aid lawyer. I suspect that before the legal aid representative had a chance to see him, within the two weeks specified, the breathalizer test would be in his favour.
Of course, I admit that is an extreme example and I recognize as well that extreme cases are not of the type on which a general policy should be based. However, when speaking of a general policy on such an important matter, I am inclined to think we should study closely the findings of the Law Reform Commission, or rather the work group that reported to the Commission on this matter. Their findings, specifically about the matter of accepting evidence obtained illegally, is that preference should be given to the present system whereby Canadian jurisprudence still gives the accused the right to defend himself adequately, to prove, if needs be, that the voluntary statement was not freely obtained, even while, on the other hand, the voluntary statement remains a fairly important instrument in the fight against crime, whether it be organized crime or crime generally.
Mr. Speaker, though I may agree with and be very favourable to the position outlined by the hon. member, I have the impression that with regard to the admissibility of evidence, he went too far. We must not forget that certain rules, certain clauses of the Criminal Code in this country and others, were passed to face specific situations, in specific cases.
In the Miranda ruling, when one reads carefully the opinion expressed by the very learned Chief Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States, one quickly realizes that he was up against a social situation that differs greatly from our own.
Charges of police brutality, of illegal imprisonment, founded accusations in the United States of extremely close examination and cross-examination, with psychological constraints of all kinds, have led the U.S. Supreme Court, and perhaps rightly in this instance, to put an end to such situation. But do such situations exist in Canada? I am inclined to believe that our Canadian tradition is

rather different from the American tradition and that we are in a position to act with much more discrimination by enacting regulations allowing to tell the judge: "It's up to you, Your Honour, to decide if in the particular case before the court it is in the interest of justice that the charge be cleared up, and if there is such an irregularity that it offends the sense of justice of Canadians in general, that this evidence should be rejected".
Such are, Mr. Speaker, the questions I am asking. All in all, I believe a forum has been especially instructed by the Parliament of Canada to look fully into that question, namely the Law Reform Commission, and I feel that we should at least wait before coming to a final decision about the kind of points raised by the hon. member, and see what are the final findings of the Law Reform Commission on a matter affecting not only the rights of the defendant but also those of society as a whole.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had a few things to say before the adjournment at five o'clock with regard to the proposal contained in the terms of this particular amendment concerning class actions. I have indicated that I, and some of my colleagues even more so, find that a class action may be one of the solutions for the better protection of the consumer. However, I will say, because I have not considered it in detail, that I do not think we have had sufficient experience.
In any event as a lawyer, I find that the form of the amendment is far from good enough to introduce into a bill that this House anticipates will become law some time this year. There are many deficiencies in it, particularly as to the ultimate solution in the event that there are awards in favour of consumers. There is no prohibition in the amendment against contingency actions.
I have discussed this matter with the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Leggatt). I would point out, subject to correction by those who may be greater authorities on constitutional law than I, that in the judicature act of the province of Ontario and I would think in the judicature acts of some of the other provinces, there are provisions which allow class actions. I think that avenue of the present law should be examined very carefully before we start stumbling in with an incomplete amendment.
With all due respect to the hon. member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez), his amendment is legally deficient. For that reason I cannot support it, although I think the idea
Combines Investigation Act
of a class action can have some application if there are adequate safeguards, not only for those who are going to be affected by it, but also for the beneficiaries. Unfortunately there are far too many remedies in this world today. Panaceas and easy solutions get peddled and bandied about in newspaper stories, headlines, and what have you, by people who do not really stop to think out the proposals. Therefore I cannot support this amendment in its present form.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DEFINITIONS, POWERS OF INVESTIGATORS, OFFENCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, having listened to the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) for many years, I expected he would find reasons not to vote for the proposed amendment. Indeed, had he announced that he was supporting the amendment I would have had to reconsider my position to see what was wrong with the amendment. But I am surprised at the minister, who has spoken so often and so eloquently about his desire to help the consumer.
It is over 50 years since Canada first had legislation purporting to regulate and control combines, certainly to prohibit the illegal getting together by business organizations to charge the public more for goods that they should be paying. That legislation was passed by a Liberal government headed by Mr. Mackenzie King, probably the most successful political leader this country has ever seen. It has been in existence, with slight amendment, for more than 50 years, during which time Liberal governments have been in office for 40 or more years. That legislation failed completely to prevent corporations from getting together and setting a price which would be high enough to permit them to make a substantial profit in a totally illegal manner at the expense of the consumer.
Over the years we have seen a large number of investigations into such illegal acts by Canadian corporations. Over the years there have been a substantial number of prosecutions. Some of them were unsuccessful; the requirements of the law were so strict that the government was unable to prove that the corporations had in fact committed an offence although it was evident to everybody but the judges that they had. In other cases the prosecution succeeded, at which time we witnessed the spectacle of the courts assessing monetary fines of $5,000, $10,000 or $20,000 on some of the largest corporations in the country.
In a recent case, as one of my hon. friends mentioned earlier in debate, a group of companies was assessed a total of $450,000 in fines. Those fines, Mr. Speaker, were completely unsuccessful in their objective, which was to prevent corporations from combining illegally to mulct the public. Indeed, as has been said many times, they were in effect a licence issued by the government authorizing those companies to steal from the public.
It is not my intention tonight to put on record the sorry performance of Canadian corporations in this area. One would see that in virtually every sector of economic life the large corporations have gotten together and knowingly broken the law. What makes one sad is the knowledge that the same corporations have been investigated, charged and convicted not once, not twice, but in many cases, three times. One can look at the paper industry, the electrical

June 10, 1975
Combines Investigation Act
industry, the coal industry. In almost every area of industry in this country the large corporations have been guilty of breaking the anti-combines law.
Let me digress by recounting a personal experience. Around 25 years ago I was a new member of the Winnipeg City Council serving on a committee which dealt with purchasing, particularly of electrical equipment. The committee had called for tenders for electrical cable. Lo and behold, there were four bids, each quoting exactly the same price per hundred foot of cable. In my innocence I thought this was perhaps an accident. I got a friend of mine, who was even newer and younger than I was, to spend an afternoon at City Hall going over the records of the purchasing committee and getting illustrations during the previous ten years of the number of times identical bids had been made. To my amazement there were several hundred cases like that.
We did not have computers in those days, but I asked a friend of mine, a professor of mathematics at the University of Manitoba, to calculate the odds on the assumption that the similarity of the bids was only accidental and that the companies had not got together to agree on a price. Well, my professor of mathematics told me the odds were several billion to one against.
I got the committee, and subsequently the City Council, by a majority of one vote-it was nine to eight-to send a letter to the federal Department of Justice asking that an inquiry be held. The federal Department of Justice looked into the matter and decided there was sufficient evidence to justify an inquiry. They appointed a prominent lawyer-he is a much more prominent lawyer at the present time; he is now Senator Goldenberg-to conduct the inquiry. What he found was that the likelihood that the companies had not got together on these bids was virtually nil. But he could find no evidence. In other words, they had put nothing in writing, so he could not recommend that the government prosecute since there was no real expectation of a prosecution succeeding. That was one of many instances in which the law did not work.
There have been dozens of cases like that. There have been dozens of other cases in which the law has worked. Here we are, in the year 1975, and we know that the laws are still being ignored. But again lo and behold, after 50 years the government is bestirring itself, and in the harbour dredging cases, for the first time if I am correct, it is not simply prosecuting the corporations concerned. It is not merely asking for a fine. It is proceeding in a manner which, if the people charged are guilty, evokes the distinct possibility that some of them may go to prison.
Suddenly in the year 1975, or maybe 1976 or '77 or '78, a corporation executive, if convicted, may go to prison. It so happens that any ordinary person who is unemployed and hungry and who steals $25 worth of groceries from a supermarket will go there tomorrow, the next day, or next week. Shall I get up and bow, or crawl on my belly and thank the minister? We are not there yet but we are certainly getting close to having one law for the rich and another for the poor.
They have had a good deal of experience with this problem in the United States. Although they have not

been much more successful in solving it than we have, for a number of years they have had in their law a provision that permits class actions. I am speaking from memory, but I do not think I am far from wrong in saying they also permit a court to assess triple damages in a case where a corporation is found guilty of breaking their anti-trust laws.
My colleague from Nickel Belt has not said, and neither has my colleague from New Westminster (Mr. Leggatt), nor I, that every corporation will be prevented from breaking the law. Of course not. But this provision will give the people of Canada, who have been mulcted probably for the last 100 years since Canada has been a country, one more defence against corporations that do break the law.
I have always assumed that my colleague from Nickel Belt, in the spectrum of our party, was on the left wing, whereas I am on the right wing, and I must admit I wondered why he was being so cautious in bringing in an amendment under which people who wanted to launch a class action would first have to get the permission of the Attorney General of Canada. I would be suspicious of almost any attorney general who is a member of the Liberal party. Although I have not discussed this with my colleague, having listened to some of the debate this afternoon I have the strong suspicion that he thought he would be able to get this very mild amendment through the House. Obviously he was wrong. I do not blame him for that; he was trying to get a slice of bread because he knew he could not get the whole loaf.
I have listened in amazement to some of the speeches made on both sides of the House. One would think that any crackpot, any lawyer who did not have a client, or any poor native in my constituency in Winnipeg could irresponsibly go to the court and start a class action, judging from what some people have said. As my colleague from New Westminster has pointed out, if that were the law and someone did choose to proceed in the direction suggested by my colleague for Nickel Belt, that person would first have to get permission to proceed from the attorney general.
Let us assume for the moment that the attorney general would do the right thing and would permit that person to go ahead with a class action. If he won his case he would be in a very excellent position. But let us not plead ignorance, Mr. Speaker. Let us realize the very simple fact that the corporations that were charged under this or any other prosecution would have, as they always have had, the best trained, most experienced, highest paid lawyers in the country defending them. I do not question their right to do that; it is the right of any person or corporation to get the best legal defence in the country if they can afford to pay the fee.
As I say, if the person or persons who initiated such a class action were successful, they would win damages, and I presume that the court would assess costs against the corporations that had broken the law. But these court cases would not be easy. They would not be over in a day or two. We can all be sure that the corporations would fight these cases from day one right through to the end, appealing to the appeal court of the province, then to the Supreme Court of Canada, and so on.
June 10, 1975

Let us ask ourselves this simple question: what happens if the class action is lost? Who would pay the costs, not only of the lawyers who represented the initiators of the action but of the lawyers representing the corporations that were charged, as well as the court costs themselves? As my colleague from New Westminster has pointed out, the costs would be paid either by the people who initiated the action or, if they did not have the money, as would be likely, by the lawyers themselves. I suggest it would be a pretty foolish lawyer who would act in a case of this kind unless he were reasonably certain that he had a pretty good case.
Let me say a word about some of the experience in the United States. There was a case there very similar to the one I have referred to in the city of Winnipeg, having to do with an illegal combine of electrical manufacturers. In the United States case I am thinking of, the issue was not electrical cable but electrical generators. The complainants won their case against the largest manufacturers of electrical generators in the United States-General Electric, Westinghouse and other large corporations. I am speaking from memory, but these companies were required to pay tens of millions, perhaps hundreds of millions of dollars by way of damages. But who was it, Mr. Speaker, who received all these damages? These damages were paid not to the individual consumers who had launched the action but to the buyers of these generators, namely, the companies that produce electric power in the United States. I presume these companies were able to show a better profit picture and used this money to reduce the price of electric power to their customers.
That is all we are asking the minister to do in this case, Mr. Speaker. He says he is prepared to consider this in phase two of the bill, but let me finish by asking this question: how long must the people of this country wait for the government to act? I forget which minister it was when this particular bill first saw the light of day many years ago, but it has taken at least four or five years to get this bill to its present stage.
I do not know as well as the minister what representations were made to him and his colleagues in cabinet, and also to the other members of his caucus, by every special interest group in this country, but one does not have to read their briefs. One need only look at the Financial Post or Financial Times week after week to discover that the business interests of this country either want no legislation at all on this subject, or as weak and meaningless legislation as possible. Why must our people wait so long before getting a class action provision in our anti-combines legislation?
I say that the experience in the United States has been a wholesome one. It has not stopped companies from getting together illegally, but it is certainly one more of the many methods that have to be used to control illegal combinations of corporations in that country. I appeal to the minister even at this late stage to listen not only to members of this party but to consumers. I do not say this in any criticism of the consumers' association, but if one compares the power and wealth of the corporations in this country with the-

That Bill C-2, to amend the Combines Investigation Act and the Bank Act and to repeal an Act to amend an Act to amend the Combines Investigation Act and the Criminal Code, be amended in Clause 12 by
(a)	striking out the word "and" at the end of line 24 on page 14
(b)	striking out line 38 on page 14 and substituting therefor "the
article in Canada, or"
(c)	adding thereto immediately after line 38 on page 14 the following
subsection
"(g) where the product is not in ample supply, order that suppliers

June 10, 1975
Combines Investigation Act
in the market share the available quantities of the product with all established customers on a pro rata basis."
He said: Mr. Speaker, this proposes to amend the section dealing with the refusal to sell where particular products or items are in short supply.
One of the most effective ways corporations have had of controlling the marketplace is by controlling the distribution of goods or items. My amendment is most concerned with the ways in which small suppliers and small retailers can be put out of business. They can be put into very dire straits when they cannot obtain supplies or items with which to conduct their business.
During the course of the committee hearings I presented a specific example which took place in the Sudbury basin, where we have the large city of Sudbury and many small communities on the outskirts. In one of those small communities we had a ski-doo dealer who was dealing in Bombardier ski-doos. His clientele was very limited and he did not handle too many of these Bombardier machines, but he was able to make a living.
In the city of Sudbury there is a large Bombardier dealer whose clientele is much larger, and he makes much more than the fellow out in the small community. Last winter, for reasons known only to the manufacturer, and incidentally I wrote to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gillespie) about this matter, the manufacturer had only so many machines and parts. He had to make a choice as to whom he would supply. He made that choice, which was to supply the large dealership in the city of Sudbury, to the detriment of the smaller dealer.
I put that example in a light which would seem most advantageous to the Bombardier company. Far be it from me to suspect that the company was trying to squeeze out this small dealer, centralize this operation in the city of Sudbury, and maximize its profits. Far be it from me to accuse the company of doing that.
Be that as it may, the small dealer in the outlying community could not get the parts or machines to supply his customers. As a result his customers first of all were inconvenienced in that those who lived in this smaller community had to drive into the city of Sudbury to get their supplies. Secondly, this small dealer lost the line because he could not service the machines he had sold and, of course, he had no new products to sell. As a result he has gone out of that line and out of business.
This is a rather sad commentary on a system that prides itself on competition and free enterprise, particularly when in fact we have these small businessmen who put their money into these lines and then, lo and behold, the investment is gone and no one cares a hoot.
The minister replied to my letter with some facetious comment about the company saying it had limited supplies. Far be it from me to suggest that we should interfere with the way Bombardier does business, but surely there is an injustice in this particular situation. This happens across the country every single day of the week.
When I presented my amendment in the committee, one of the members felt that if my amendment were carried by the committee it would create an injustice, and he outlined a typical case. He said:
-we will say, one dealing totally in imported products and one dealing

in a domestic product. If that particular product became in short supply under the terms of Mr. Rodriguez' amendment what he is saying is that the domestic supplier would then be compelled to supply his product to the fellow who is normally importing it, and when the imported product comes back into the marketplace again then he would drop the domestic supplier. This is the actuality of what you are saying.
Those were the words of my colleague, the hon. member for Halton-Wentworth (Mr. Kempling). He raised a very good point. As soon as he had done that, I tried to do what I think the minister should be doing. He should be taking advantage of the ideas put forward to strengthen this bill. That is one of the things I want to stress to the House that we are attempting to do in proposing amendments to this bill.
From the moment we embarked on a consideration of this bill we began attempting to strengthen it, making it better and more useful to the consumers. We have observed a very positive approach throughout the hearings in committee, as well as during the debate on second reading. We are now at the report stage trying to be very positive in strengthening the bill.
Keeping in mind the criticism of my colleague, I tried to rephrase the amendment to include the words which would satisfy his criticism. My amendment now states in part:
(g) where the product is not in ample supply, order that suppliers in the market share the available quantities of the product with all established customers on a pro rata basis.
The customer would have to be an established customer of that particular supplier, and .could not be someone who is importing a foreign article in competition with another domestic retailer who is selling the domestic product. The customer concerned would have to be an established customer of that particular company. I see the hon. member nodding his head vertically, so I suspect he agrees with that suggestion for a change.
In criticizing this amendment the minister previously asked how the available supplies will be shared. The amendment states that the available supplies would be shared on a pro rata basis. That obviously means a ratio based on the size of the business, for instance how large it is. That would seem to me to be a very fair way. Surely the intent is not to develop large and powerful conglomerates in our society. I am no defender of the free enterprise system because I have said, time and time again, that there is no free enterprise system, that this is a hoax, and that we are dealing with a contrived, controlled, and administered market. Surely we do not want very large and powerful suppliers. Is that what the game is all about, that the strongest will survive and crush the small fellow?
I have heard many pious statements about the small businessman and the help he needs. Indeed I have heard hon. members of this House say that the small businessman is the backbone of society. He is. We might consider how we treat the small businessman. I suggest that my amendment goes some way toward alleviating the problems which face the small businessman. I gave the example of Bombardier.
When the small retailer comes up against the powerful and big, he is supposed to close up his tent and steal away.
June 10, 1975

Surely that is not the approach we should take in this country. When politicians speak on the election platforms, surely this is not the approach they would take. Surely that is not what is expected of us as legislators. Surely we must have laws which give the small businessman an opportunity to obtain supplies in order to service the customers he has.
I do not believe we should consider legislation of any kind which in any way interferes with the operations of the small businessman when he is attempting to earn a living. I should not be the one making the argument for these people. Surely all these corporate defenders should be making this case, but I suspect they are the defenders of the large and corpulent corporations, the affluent corporations rather than the small businessman.
Since I believe I have made my point very effectively I would ask members of the House to consider very carefully the logic I have put forward in this amendment. Indeed the hon. member for Cape Breton-East Richmond (Mr. Hogan) said there are small businessmen in his riding who are faced with the same problems. He endorsed my amendment, and said it would certainly come to grips with some of the problems in his particular riding.
In conclusion I wish to point out that the minister took a very callous view of the small dealer in my riding. When I raised the question with him in committee and we locked horns on this particular amendment, he suggested that the dealer to whom I referred should get another line, such as lawn mowers. No one who knows Sudbury would suggest that such a dealer should deal in lawn mowers. That would be like a death knell. If there were grass to cut one could do very well in the lawn mower business. The minister took a very callous view when he suggested that this small dealer get out of skidoos and go into lawn mowers. That is not the kind of comment one would expect from a minister who is supposed to be concerned about the consumers and the kind of deal they get in the marketplace. The way we treat the small businessmen reflects on the consumer.
I mentioned once before today that the small retailer passes on to the consumer the same treatment he receives in his relationship with the large corporate suppliers. That is a very dangerous trend. Once again it is part of the philosophy on which I touched earlier today whereby one takes the position that he will do to others what has been done to him. That is a very bad attitude.
I would like to see an atmosphere created where whatever the available supplies may be, if for some reason or other the materials necessary for the manufacture of a product should be in short supply and the manufacturer can produce only half of his normal production, they would be shared equally in the market where he has established dealers. This would refer only to established dealers and not to anyone who should come on the scene. The crux of this is that the small dealer should be able to have his supplies in order to stay in business and deal in the marketplace. This is very important if we are looking for justice in the marketplace.
The other point I wish to raise concerns available supplies. I realize that in the legislation the minister has introduced he has taken a tough line in respect of refusal to deal, but if a large corporation does not wish to deal
Combines Investigation Act
with a particular customer it has many ways in which to squeeze him out of the marketplace. One way would be, if a manufacturer had his factory in Oakville or Port Credit and the dealer were located in Sudbury, he could ship his goods via the Suez Canal, or he could send them by mail which would probably be effective enough to get them to the dealer ten months later. During that time the dealer would be unable to supply his customers. Then in another situation the dealer might open up a box and find that the items were broken, or that somehow or other the wrong items were packed and shipped to him. In the meantime his customers have to wait and, as a result, the small dealer goes down the drain.
This amendment calls on the corporations to be a little socialistic in their thinking for a change. The amendment calls on the corporation to share what available supplies there are with their established customers on a pro rata basis. Not even my colleague from Halton-Wentworth can deny the justice in this amendment. I call on members of the House to take a very hard look at this amendment and consider the justice of it. In closing, Mr. Speaker, I call on all members of the House to vote in favour of this amendment.

speechtext:
This amendment really makes a pretty weak case. The hon. member is taking an individual example from his riding of a small distributor of snowmobiles who found himself in difficulty in obtaining parts for snowmobiles in his area. I do not think there is anyone in the NDP who has ever been in business, or knows anything about it. If there were someone like that, he would not talk like this.
I do not suppose there is anyone who has been in business who at one time or another has not had some supplier come to him and indicate that there would be a short supply of a product the following winter, spring, or some time in the year. Whether a businessman reacts is his responsibility. It has happened in my business, and I know of hundreds of other people who are faced with the same problem.
Suppliers have come to me and asked me to place orders two years in advance so that I would have ample supplies on hand, and if I chose not to place those orders, then I did not obtain the supplies.
What the amendment is really doing is suggesting that the government legislate inefficiency. It is suggesting that if a product for one reason or another becomes in short supply, the government should decree through the Restricted Trade Practices Commission that all the suppliers in that particular field share their production jointly with established customers. I do not know what an established customer is. The amendment does not say "the established customers of that particular supplier." It just says "established customers," so it might be assumed that anyone who is in the field selling that particular product is an established customer, and that is a pretty weak case.

June 10, 1975
Combines Investigation Act
If one is running a business, one has to take chances. Inventory and market must be considered. If a product is going to be in short supply, perhaps inventory should be increased so that customers can be served. If that decision is not made, I do not think one should come crying to the government, because of a lack of foresight, because he did not look far enough ahead, because he did not have the money, because of lack of space or whatever reason, and demand that it legislate and make all the suppliers sell this product which is in short supply. That is the way business operates.
Suppliers give companies a proposition. If those companies turn it down, if they do not act on the suggestion of the supplier, if they do not analyse the suggestion properly-if their analysis proves that the supplier is wrong and they do not act on it, they are all right-but if the supplier is right and companies do not act on his advice, I do not think they should come to the government and ask to be bailed out because of error in judgment, or because of lack of foresight with regard to adequate space for servicing machines which are sold, or whatever the case may be. I do not think companies should demand that the government get after a particular manufacturing concern and make it share all its products equally on a pro rata basis with all the people in the marketplace.
As the hon. member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez) has already stated, at the committee I mentioned the case of a distributor of raw steel or sheet steel buying his products off-shore. This matter was brought to our attention, I believe, by the president of the Steel Company of Canada when he was before the committee, and I agreed with his position. Why should he share his steel supplies with someone who normally imports steel and does not normally use the domestic market? The frivolous change in this amendment with regard to established customers does not cover that situation at all.
The same thing exists in the rubber industry. We discussed the rubber industry last week or the week before, when there was an opposition day with regard to the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce, and here we have a situation where in the last year something like 60 per cent of the tires sold were imported into Canada. We recognize that there was a serious strike in a couple of the industries, a shortage of supply, and many other things. It could be a strike, it could be a shipping problem, lack of money, lack of capacity, or a number of things, but to suggest that the established manufacturers of a product share their production on a pro rata basis is just ridiculous.
The same applies to distribution. One could say that any product imported into Canada would fall under the meaning of the word "product". When someone who has foresight, who sees a market, who sees a potential, fills his warehouse full of products and all of a sudden there is a great demand for that product, through his foresight his warehouse is full. His competitor down the road did not have the foresight, but under this amendment the person who had this foresight would have to share his available supplies with the person who did not have the foresight to look ahead and see what was required.
I am always amazed at the way the socialist members in this House come down on corporations. Every third word
[Mr. Kempling.j
they utter is about corporations this and corporations that. It is really rather sickening. In the twenty-ninth parliament we heard about the corporate rip-off and all the other things which go with it. Those hon. members are just repeating the same nonsense over and over again. They view a corporation as some sort of corporate ogre trying to shaft consumers at every opportunity.

speechtext: Right on.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DEFINITIONS, POWERS OF INVESTIGATORS, OFFENCES
speechtext: That is just a lot of nonsense. The average corporation in this country, large or small, which manufactures or distributes products does so for one reason to supply and sell those products, and it will do everything it can to continue that process. I get a little sick of hearing that story from my hon. friends to my left. They really do not have much to go on, so they go after corporations. Who answers for corporations? Not very many people.

speechtext: You do.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DEFINITIONS, POWERS OF INVESTIGATORS, OFFENCES
speechtext:
I am really surprised that the hon. member moves this amendment today. I thought that at committee this legislation was thoroughly discussed. I suggest that all the hon. member is trying to do is to stall this legislation as long as he can. I do not think he wants it to pass. If he had any concern for this legislation he would not have moved a frivolous amendment such as this.
What is ample supply, and who is going to judge what it is? What rules is the Restricted Trade Practices Commission to use with regard to ample supply? What is meant by "share the available quantities," and what are "established customers"? These terms are broad and have very little meaning or effect. They are nebulous words. What is ample supply of a product?
Most people in business of any substance, large or small, project ahead. In my small business I look ahead to what my inventory requirements will be 12 months or 24 months hence, and I plan accordingly. Even a grocer has to plan what supplies he thinks he will require, and if he does not have the right things on his shelves, tough luck. That is his baby. He has the opportunity to buy, and if he does not take advantage of it, that is his tough luck and he does not have much business.
I would recommend that my colleagues not support this amendment. I think the hon. member moved it so that he could put a few words on the record. He wanted to repeat his story again and take a crack at corporations, which is really all his party is here to do anyway.
This is not a good amendment. It is not worded properly. It does not have much substance to it, and I recommend that we do not support it. At least I certainly will not support it.

Madam Speaker, my amendment is again put forward in order to clarify what seems to be a very loose subclause of this bill. The relevant part of clause 12 of the bill, being the last five lines on page 17 and the first four lines on page 18, reads as follows:
(4) The commission shall not make an order under this section where, in its opinion,
(a) exclusive dealing or market restriction is or will be engaged in
only for a reasonable period of time to facilitate entry of a new
supplier of a product into a market or of a new product into a

There is a sort of holding period until a new supplier or a new product enters a market, but there ought to be more leeway. I wanted to clarify this subclause so that we would know what we are dealing with in terms of the time element.
The hon. member for Halton-Wentworth (Mr. Kem-pling) said that my amendments were not specific, but this one is. This would give the Restrictive Trade Practices Commission an idea of how long a reasonable period of time is. In the opinion of some suppliers it could be 50 years, and other suppliers might wish that it was never. My amendment to put in a time frame is very important to this bill. I therefore ask hon. members to support the amendment which clarifies "reasonable period of time".

speechtext: I do not want to be the one who is always speaking against the hon. member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez), but with this amendment he shows that he does not know very much about business, how products are introduced to the market, or indeed anything at all about retailing.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DEFINITIONS, POWERS OF INVESTIGATORS, OFFENCES
speechtext: He is against the small businessman.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DEFINITIONS, POWERS OF INVESTIGATORS, OFFENCES
speechtext:
Sure he is-he is against the world, the corporations-you name it, he is against it. A new product introduced to the marketplace may take five years or eight years to become established; it depends on what is already there. I do not think the parliament of Canada should be involved in determining the period that should be allowed for the introduction of a product. It should be left to the Restrictive Trade Practices Commission to look at the industry concerned and determine whether the time allowed for the introduction of a product is reasonable and whether certain protections are given under this act.
All sorts of things could happen in one year. We saw how wheat shipments in western Canada were held up because of weather. There could be strikes, or anything else that would use up a good portion of the year. To my way of thinking this amendment does not add anything to the bill but makes it more restrictive. Products that have not even been designed yet will occupy the shelves in the next decade, and if we pass restrictive legislation it would not do much to help them get under way.
I cannot support the amendment. The hon. member is nit picking. I think his amendment is out of place and should not be accepted. We talked about it in committee and thought it was restrictive. I think we should leave the bill as loose as possible in this regard and give the Restrictive Trade Practices Commission room to move if any problems arise when a new product arrives in the marketplace. I recommend to my colleagues that we not support the amendment.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DEFINITIONS, POWERS OF INVESTIGATORS, OFFENCES
speechtext:
That Bill C-2, an act to amend the Combines Investigation Act and the Bank Act and to repeal and act to amend an act to amend the Combines Investigation Act and the Criminal Code, be amended in Clause 12 by adding to subclause 31.4(5) immediately after line 34 on page 18 the following:
"(c) companies, partnerships, sole proprietorships, and persons are affiliated if between them there exists a contract for a definite or indefinite period, in which one grants to another the right to use a trade mark or trade name to identify the grantee's business related to the sale or distribution of commodities or services pursuant to a marketing plan or system prescribed substantially by the grantor." and by striking out the word "and" at the end of paragraph (a) and adding the word "and" at the end of paragraph (b) thereof.
He said: Madam Speaker, the motion before the House is significant for the franchising industry of Canada. I hope to convince all hon. members to support this motion. I earnestly hope the minister will stand up at the appropriate time and say if the government intends to support the motion or intends to stick to the position it adopted in the committee, a position of refusing to accept this amendment which could be of tremendous advantage to the franchise industry of the country.
Some members considering this bill in the finance committee had some unfortunate experiences. Although we were given many learned and extensive briefs dealing with certain sections of the bill, the Liberal members on the committee virtually ignored the briefs. Time and again, after we had referred to briefs, asked questions about them, and asked why the minister would not accede to the requests contained in those briefs, we were told nothing. Liberal members did not ask any questions about points raised in those briefs.
The committee received 90 briefs and heard many applications when we dealt with clause 31.4 of the competition bill. Altogether some 37 briefs were submitted on the question with which I want to deal this evening. Despite the presentation of those many briefs I must confess that Liberal members on the committee made no meaningful contribution to the discussion of that clause which motion No. 5 seeks to amend. They contributed little, even though briefs were submitted by firms like Abitibi Paper Company Ltd., which spoke for many other notable companies in Canada. Briefs were also submitted by Allied Beauty Association, Canadian Association of Equipment Distributors, the Canadian Bar Association, Canadian Council of Furniture Manufacturers, Canadian
[The Acting Speaker (Mrs. Morin).]
Daily Newspaper Publishers Association, Canadian Federation of Independent Business, and others.
I emphasize that these briefs touched specifically on those clauses of Bill C-2 we now propose to amend. Briefs were also submitted by the Canadian Institute of Chartet-ed Accountants, Canadian Institute of Plumbing and Heating, Canadian Machine Tool Distributors Association, Canadian Manufacturers' Association, The Canadian Real Estate Association, Canadian Soft Drink Association, Canadian Tire Corporation Limited, Central Contract Bottlers Association, Coca-Cola Ltd., Comcheq Services Limited, Consumers' Association of Canada, Dominion Dairies Limited, Dominion Foundries and Steel Limited, and others.
All those briefs expressed varying degrees of alarm at the provisions of clause 31.4, the clause which we hope to amend at the report stage.
Included in the various briefs submitted were briefs by Grocery Products Manufacturers of Canada, Imperial Oil Limited, the National Automotive Trades Association of Canada, Patent and Trademark Institute of Canada, Reinforcing Steel Institute of Ontario, Saint John Beverages Limited, Sun Oil Company Limited, 3M Limited, Toilet Goods Manufacturers Association, Western Contract Bottlers Association, and others.
Liberal members deliberately ignored the efforts which these concerns had made to impress upon the government the necessity for changing proposed clause 31.4. They voted down every effort which was made to accede to requests contained in those briefs.
As hon. members no doubt know, the bill before us has been considered by a committee of the other place. It suggested many amendments. We have asked the minister repeatedly to comment on amendments the other place has proposed. Almost without exception he has shown little interest in what members of the other place have said.
At present we are dealing with franchising. The interim report of the Senate Standing Committee on Banking, Trade and Commerce, contained in issue No. 33 of the proceedings of that committee, says on page 33.9:
An important instrument in the life of the business community is the franchise agreement, e.g., an agreement whereby the supplier permits the customer to use his trade mark or trade name in connection with the customer's business, on condition that certain standards with respect to the operation of such business designed to protect the good will associated with the trade mark or trade name are maintained. These arrangements permit a decentralization of economic activity which is in the interests of both the consumers and the small businessman. However, they may necessarily involve some degree of exclusive dealing, tied selling and marked restriction practices.
Your committee recommends that an amendment be made to make it clear that no order under section 31.4 shall apply to such practices where they are carried on in accordance with a franchise agreement as described above.
Despite the observations of the independent committee of the other place, the minister has refused to accept the amendment before us, an amendment which, if passed, would ensure that franchising is not undermined in this country.
The Independent Grocers' Alliance, IGA, presented a thoughtful brief which points out at least one inconsistency. An affiliated company is defined as one which, among other things, is 51 per cent owned by another company.
June 10, 1975

The net result is that IGA will be in competition with wholly owned groceries, such as Dominion Stores, which will not be caught by the provisions of clause 31.4 of the competition bill. If a grocery store distributes groceries under a franchise, it will come under the provisions of clause 31.4, whereas a grocery store which is a wholly owned distributor, in the sense that Dominion Stores is a wholly owned distributor, will not be affected by the provisions of this clause.
The IGA brief says in part, beginning on page 6:
Some of the proposed sections of Bill C-2 discriminate against the voluntary group system, in that they contain prohibitions, and trade practices which may become subject to prohibition, which would apply to the voluntary group system, but which at the same time would not apply to the chain distributor. These proposed sections are of major importance, and in our opinion can threaten the very existence of the voluntary group system as it exists today.
In their brief the IGA also point out, and I quote:
Section 31.4 deals with "exclusive dealing", "market restriction", and "tied selling." Under the section, the commission may prohibit the practice of a supplier of a product requiring a customer to deal primarily in products supplied by or designated by the supplier or his nominee.
They point out that when you link that with the exclusive dealing provisions, you are going at the very heart of franchising in this country. The net result is that if the Restrictive Trade Practices Commission were to find that there is a significant lessening of competition in the market notwithstanding the fact that a franchisee may be involved, they may make an order that in fact may mean that franchisee can no longer carry on in business, notwithstanding the fact also that, with the same position, a company owned store will not be open to attack by the Restrictive Trade Practices Commission.
It is particularly unfortunate, and I suggest giving the benefit of the doubt, that the civil servants who are proposing this provision, and the minister who is acceding to their request, do not properly understand the functioning of franchisees and franchisors in this country. If they did understand the process I am sure they would see the danger of having these clauses cover the very substance of franchising arrangements.
I personally believe that it is better to have a franchisee who, to the extent he is able to operate his own business, does so. He is an entrepreneur. I suggest it is better for the government and we parliamentarians to encourage that type of individual inititative and entrepreneurship than to be discouraging it and forcing more and more small businessmen to give up their franchising arrangement with no alternative but to end up as wholly owned subsidiaries of other concerns. In truth, they simply act as employed managers for other companies in whatever business they choose to be active. That is what is at stake here tonight.
The government, for reasons I have indicated or perhaps for other reasons, has chosen to deny to the franchising industry, as they have spelled it out in their briefs, any exception with regard to the provisions of this bill, in spite of the fact the exemptions have been extended to certain of the large corporations that our friends to the left like to speak about so often.
Combines Investigation Act
I stated that Imperial Oil Limited submitted a brief. I believe it is important to note certain sections of it. At page 13 they state:
As we have stated above we believe that an exemption should be provided for franchises which involve a degree of "tied selling"-
I would emphasize that. Imperial Oil then point out:
This was contemplated in Bill C-256 which provided in section 40(2) that: "a practice is not a restrictive practice where it meets one or more of the following conditions: (a) the practice is engaged in between or among affiliated companies; (b) in the case of tied sales, i) there exists a technological relationship, between the tied commodity or service and the tying commodity or service that makes the practice necessary to the satisfactory performance or use of the tying commodity or service; ii) the practice is incidental to, and reasonably necessary for, the purpose of enabling two or more persons to carry on business under a common trade description or designation and is not significantly restrictive of competition,"-
All we are asking is that that type of accommodation be put back into the bill as it was originally contemplated when Bill C-256 was introduced in this House some time ago. It is a simple matter. The simple matter is this: do we believe in the franchising industry in Canada? Do we believe it is preferable that groups of businessmen can get together in an association and have the advantage of multiple buying, advertising, and a known management system worked out?
Do we believe it is worthwhile to encourage businessmen to get together and go into these franchising or franchisee relationships, or do we agree with the government's position to date? It would sooner see a greater concentration of business in the sense of those who are now active in the franchising business deciding it is not worthwhile to live with these types of government regulations and it would be preferable to exempt them by simply taking over the franchisees they have been working for up to the present time. That is the problem that faces us.
If hon. members support my motion, this problem will be relieved. This motion will make it clear that not only is it 51 per cent or more companies that are designated as affiliated and exempted from the act. It will also make it clear that franchisees in the relationship spelled out in the motion will also be exempted from the provisions of the act. They will be able to carry on business free of any type of indiscriminate order that might be made by the Restrictive Trade Practices Commission.
I would refer hon. members to the Canadian Bar Association brief. They make what I believe is a very good case as to the danger that will arise if this clause is allowed to remain in its present form. I will not take the time of the House to read the various paragraphs in their brief. Presumably the minister is well aware of it. It is something he should deal with tonight.
The simple question is whether the minister will put some accommodation into this clause to assist the franchisors and franchisees who have come before this House asking that they be given some relief from what they think will be an unbearable provision if it is wielded by the Restrictive Trace Practices Commission. In short, will the minister accede to their request?
Having said that, we must also look at the other side. What is the minister trying to overcome here? What is the magnitude of the problem? Frankly I was surprised when in committee I asked the minister how many complaints

June 10, 1975
Combines Investigation Act
the department had received concerning, for example, clause 31.2, and he replied 200. When I asked over how long a period, he stated since the department was formed. As we know, the department was formed as something rather innocent back in 1968. That means that in a seven-year period they have had an average of 30 complaints a year, and this has given rise to the provisions that we find in 31.2 of the bill before us.
When we reached 31.4, I asked the minister how many complaints had been received that gave rise to the provisions in 31.4. If I was startled under 31.2, I was very startled under 31.4. I found out there had not even been as many as 200 complaints. There was no great problem the minister could show to the committee concerning a large number of complaints to his department demanding that action be taken. In short, I believe that the provisions throughout 31.4 have been inspired by over-eager, overanxious civil servants wanting to spread their wings and get into new and perhaps unexplored avenues that they have no business getting into.
If the minister insists on pushing it through, as he did in committee, we have no choice but to go along. That is the way of the brutal majority. But surely we can plead with the minister not to trample indiscriminately to the ground a budding franchise industry in this country-in the United States its counterpart handles about 25 per cent of the total merchandising. It is a question of leaving those independent entrepreneurs to do their thing. If it is competition that the minister is looking for, let him not inadvertently impede competition as he will do if he persists in this action.

That raises a very serious question, Madam Speaker, and I do not say it with tongue in cheek. I say it very seriously because I have heard the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens), that great defender of the corporate sector. As a matter of fact it was his great defence of the corporate sector which made me so avid in my defence of the consumer.
