The hon. member is arguing that we exempt franchises from the provisions of exclusive dealing, market restriction or tied selling. Considering all the exceptions that the minister is prepared to put in here-he has them all listed including the franchises-then against whom will these restrictions be held? Who is left when you have excluded the franchises, you have excluded the subsidiaries, you have excluded all the oil companies, and you have excluded those who are affiliated or those who are sole partnerships or joint partnerships? Who is left after we exempt the franchises?
You know, Madam Speaker, this great defence of the franchises makes me say I do not know where or to whom the hon. member was speaking, because I listened to the dealers, the men who operate the gas stations, the Imperial Oil stations and the Gulf stations and the Texaco stations, and there you can hear a tale of tied selling like you have never heard before. To assume that somehow or other there are all sorts of competitive factors at work in the marketplace is not to understand what is going on in the marketplace.
I, too, listened to the National Association of Tobacco and Confectionery Distributors. They appeared before the committee. The hon. member for York-Simcoe did not mention them. And, boy, did they ever rip into the National Grocers and all those outfits, the National Grocers owned by the western outfit, complaining about the way they are treated, complaining about the practices used by those large distributors in respect of the small retailers and small wholesalers. Those are the tales that are told. To make it sound as if this corporate group which appeared before the committee were all so innocent is to underplay the whole situation.
I have no use, either, for these exceptions the minister is making with respect to exclusive dealing, market restriction or tied selling and I say a pox on both their houses! That is setting up legislation, Madam Speaker, and then leaving it standing like a scarecrow in a field. It isn't effective in scaring off anything at all. In fact it does not apply to anything. To say you have consumer protection in legislation is a farce. Against whom is it going to be applied?
June 10, 1975

The hon. member for York-Simcoe wants to exclude franchises. That is one of the areas that is very seriously affected with respect to tied selling, whereby the company supplying the materials says that before you get the material you will have to carry this and this. There are many examples of that, and during committee hearings we tried to bring up specific examples.
One of the examples we used was that of the fellow who has a dealership for Imperial Oil. He is pumping gas and has his own garage. The guy is quite happy pumping Imperial gas. If you want to say something you can take the floor. In effect, Madam Speaker, this little dealer is being tied with respect to obtaining Imperial gas and has to take all the other things. Well, he has no choice in the matter. He is stuck. So it is with the consumer.
A consumer goes to a particular dealer who may be representing Gulf Oil, and maybe he does not want the particular battery the Gulf Oil dealer has to offer. Maybe the consumer wants an Atlas battery. Well, the fellow says he hasn't got an Atlas battery because he carries Gulf products. Now the consumer has to go maybe across town-we all don't live in large cities-and so in effect the consumer does not have a choice of products in his neighbourhood gas dealership. I do not understand this great defence of the kind of monopoly system that operates. For Heaven's sake I could just imagine this debate taking place right back maybe 60, 70 or 100 years ago, and if there were no legislation at all with respect to monopolies there are members in this House who would be quite happy.
I do not believe the hon. member for York-Simcoe, or any other member in this House should underestimate the ability of Imperial-Esso, IBM, Gulf Oil, and Sun Life Insurance to work around the legislation that is passed by this House. Indeed I have a strong suspicion that it is purposely designed for smart lawyers, corporate lawyers and others to move in on. For example, proposed section 31.4 opens up a whole avenue and permits an elephant to walk right through the legislation. Certainly any smart corporate operator in Canada can get around the legislation. There is nothing in the bill that a self-respecting corporation could not get around. I said that on second reading, and I say it again now. It is as much "huffery and puffery" as a pinch of snuff. speechtext:
I should like to say a few words about this franchising provision in the bill and the amendment of my colleague, the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens). I am wondering whether the minister and his officials have closely thought out the implications of the bill and have really considered this amendment. Franchising operations commence every day. There are all sorts of small companies that go into business. They get a line of products or design a line of products, or they invent something, and immediately want to sell it, and they go across the country establishing franchise operators for that product.
I have been involved in this business for 20 to 25 years and I know exactly how it works. You establish a franchise operator and in some cases advertise on a national scale. You tie your franchise operators together by getting them to agree to service the product if it comes into their area from another area. It is quite involved. These people are individual entrepreneurs.
What is happening in the country today? I do not know whether the minister and his officials realize it, but there is building in this country a tremendous service industry, and franchising is part of that industry. Corporations move to Canada from the United States as well as from Britain, and buy up the operations of small entrepreneurs. They do not come within the Foreign Investment Review Act because they do not have the necessary assets to be considered by the Foreign Investment Review Board. But these small companies are being built into giant corporations across the country. I am not going to name them because I do not think it would be proper to do so; they have not done anything illegal.
The thing that concerns us in this regard is that this type of operation is not covered by the legislation at all. There are company owned service centres spread all across

June 10, 1975
Combines Investigation Act
the country, and this sort of thing is growing day by day. An entrepreneur enters into a franchise agreement to sell a product in a given area, and in direct competition with him is one of these company owned operations. One is covered under the act, the other is not. I suggest we should look at this very closely. There should be some measure of protection given the franchisee in this country, yet he is not covered under the legislation at all.
My colleague from York-Simcoe made reference to the briefs submitted to the committee. I have to concur with him; I do not think the minister's officials, let alone the Liberal members who sat on the committee, really looked at these briefs and at what they said about franchise operations.
A good way to build up a business is through franchise operators. As I say, I have been through it myself. Basically you go around the country looking for good, solid operations, and you negotiate an agreement with them to franchise a product and sell and service it. This involves demonstrating the product, showing it at national and trade shows of one type and another across the country, and in some cases national advertising. You supply these operators with literature and go through the whole process of starting them up in business. Yet no protection whatever is afforded by this legislation.
Corporate groups are moving into this country and expanding because, I suggest, they are sheltered under this type of legislation. The Sherman anti-trust laws on vertical integration are very stringent in the United States, but here in Canada they see an open market. I learned at a meeting I attended a few weeks ago that a British firm is presently in the process of getting a franchise from a Swedish manufacturer to distribute a line of products in this country. These products will be distributed totally through company owned operations. In some cases Canadian entrepreneurs will be bought out. In other cases straight company owned operations will be set up. As I see this legislation as presently framed, it comes down on the side of company owned operations and against small franchisees.

I listened to him and tried to meet his concern in the committee, but I think there is an honest disagreement between that hon. member and myself on this question. I think he is a little too sensitive to the implication of this particular clause in dealing with franchises.
I see no likelihood that the provision will prevent the operation of any useful franchise operator. I have said in committee, and I repeat here tonight, that exclusive dealing which may substantially lessen competition has been prohibited since 1940 in the United States, and I know of no nation where there are so many successful franchise operations. We in Canada are not against franchise operations just as the Americans are not against such operations.
On the other hand, if a firm does operate in such a way that competition is substantially lessened by a requirement it imposes, I submit to you it is hard to justify refusing to disturb the situation simply because it is a franchise operation. This provision has been amended in committee in order to meet many of the points presented in the many briefs, and we have made some amendments in order to clarify the clause to make sure it is really getting at the heart of the question. But to accept such an amendment would, I submit to you, Madam Speaker, cut the heart out of the clause. Therefore I do not accept it.

subtopic: TRANSPORT-TOLLS ON ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY-POSSIBILITY OF INCREASE

speakeroldname: Mr. A. D. Alkenbrack (Frontenac-Lennox and Addington):
subtopic: TRANSPORT-TOLLS ON ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY-POSSIBILITY OF INCREASE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the question I debate tonight is pursuant to my oral question asked in the House on Wednesday, March 26. I asked the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) to allow no increase in tolls on the St. Lawrence Seaway.
I have been a free trader and it hurts me, and millions of other Canadians, to see the tolls and fees for vessels using the Seaway steadily increase, year by year, in the history of the operation of this great utility.
Since first coming here 13 years ago I have been a consistent protagonist of a free Seaway because that is the only way to bring commerce into the heartland of Canada and to serve best the economic interests of all of Canada; that is, to have the seaway as open as we possibly can to the commerce of the world.
This is especially important to us now because of the generally poor condition of our economy and the stagflation we are experiencing as a nation, with a combination of serious unemployment and rampant inflation. I have put my views on behalf of a freer St. Lawrence Seaway on the record more than once in the past, as early as 1966-67, at pages 5552 and 5553 of Hansard for May 22, and again in 1971 at pages 7298 and 7299 of Hansard for June 23. I still oppose any further increase in tolls on this waterway.
Although we do not have the time tonight to go into the detail, I am sure the House will agree that the current year, 1975, certainly is a very poor time to place further charges on the users of the Seaway, which would only make our international trade situation worse, increase the costs of our imports, and at the same time increase the cost of our vital export trade, which would tend to price us as a nation out of world markets. This has gone far enough.
6638

June 10, 1975
Adjournment Debate
I am alarmed when I read statements such as the following which is contained in Canadian Transportation and Distribution Management, March, 1975:
A vessel with 20,000 tons of general cargo would have to pay $18,000 to get from the St. Lambert Lock near Montreal to Lake Ontario, under present Seaway tolls. Should these be raised 27 per cent, as the Carr Report suggested in 1971, this would add another $5,000 to the charge: no small change in anyone's money.
As the accompanying table indicates, Seaway tonnage in 1974 was down 25 per cent over 1973 and, ominously, bulk cargos declined as much as general merchandise shipments.
The following are the statistics quoted in this magazine: Bulk cargo in 1973 was 48.50 million tons. In 1974 it was 36.14 million tons, a reduction of 25 per cent. Iron ore in terms of tonnage slumped 13 per cent. Grain slumped 33 per cent; oil and petroleum products slumped 49 per cent. There are fractions involved here but they are small. Other items slumped 16 per cent. General cargo in total tonnage was down 23 per cent. Manufactured iron and steel was down 20 per cent. Containers were down 51 per cent and others were down 22 per cent. The total cargo loss from 1973 to 1974 through the Seaway was 25 per cent. This magazine article states further:
Whatever his proposals, Ottawa has three basic options in reaching a decision about them.
It can raise Seaway tolls, as suggested in the 1971 report by D. W. Carr.
It can retire the Seaway debt and accumulated interest as a federal obligation, and hope the Seaway profits will continue to at least balance the Welland Canal losses.
It can retire the Seaway debt and accumulated interest as a federal obligation, and raise Seaway tolls, as Normandeau has suggested.
Or, it can subsidize the operation of the whole Authority, allowing free, or nearly free, passage along the Seaway and into Lake Erie for all vessels.
Now, Madam Speaker, I recommend to you and the House a meld of the last two recommendations; that is, that the people of Canada retire the Seaway debt and accumulated interest as a federal obligation, and subsidize the operation of the whole authority in the same way we subsidize the railways, and allow free or nearly free passage along the whole of the Seaway. In doing so we would in a short time correct and cure many of our economic ills in this country. We could create here in the heartland of Canada an economy which would grow and prosper. Such measures would fight and defeat unemployment in our area. If we did this, our economy and our creative activity could become the envy of the world.
The Seaway serves directly an area of about 1,200,000 square miles, with a population of about 65 million. The area produces about 78 per cent of North American steel, as well as one-half in value of North American manufacturing. From it comes 40 per cent of the continent's food for both human and animal consumption. It generates about 34 per cent of the capital investment used in both Canada and the United States respectively, and receives about 40 per cent of the total freight traffic moved in each country.
These impressive but wholly factual statistics indicate clearly the immensity of the asset which the seaway is to the Canadian economy as a whole. But it must always be remembered that this immensity is economic. Therefore it is vulnerable to such economic forces as inflation, unemployment, and rising competitive costs, and among the

rising costs which have to be considered no item is more important than transportation. This is the basic truth which the bureaucrats in Ottawa are forgetting.
I plead with the government not to yield to the demands and recommendations of the Ottawa bureaucrats to increase tolls and lock charges on the St. Lawrence Seaway, and to make its decision for a freer and thus more prosperous Seaway and a freer and more prosperous Canadian nation.

speakeroldname: Mr. Joseph-Philippe Guay (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Regional Economic Expansion):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion; Whip of the Liberal Party
subtopic: TRANSPORT-TOLLS ON ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY-POSSIBILITY OF INCREASE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am sure that the hon. member will admit that the government has always considered the St. Lawrence Seaway as an important cog in the maintenance of the economic health of the country. Since 1959 this fact has become more and more obvious to both Canada and the United States. The Seaway is essential not only for the goods we import from other countries, but it is critical for our exports of wheat and other raw material and finished products.
Since 1959 the debt of the Seaway has consistently increased because revenues often do not permit the authority to pay off even the interest on the original capital expenditures. In 1970 the United States took measures to rationalize the debt structure of their portion of the seaway, thus helping them maintain and improve facilities where necessary.
As the hon. member is aware, we are revising the whole transportation policy. It is obvious that the St. Lawrence Seaway is an integral part of Canada's transportation system, and it is obvious that there is a problem of re-financing with regard to the Seaway.
The Ministry of Transport has been studying this matter for several months now, and it is hoped that a submission to Cabinet will go forward in the near future. However, I do not think it is possible to anticipate what Cabinet will decide when it addresses itself to this question. I can assure the hon. member that whatever decision is taken, if indeed Cabinet decides that changes are in order, will be in the best interests of the country.

speechtext:
John MacEachen, Allan's brother. He was killed in a car accident.
This afternoon the hon. member for Riviere-du-Loup-Temiscouata (Mr. Gendron) asked the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) a question relative to the development of the super port at Gros Cacouna on the St. Lawrence near Riviere-du-Loup. My supplementary question
June 10, 1975

was designed to bring to the attention of the House that there is strong potential competition between Gros Cacou-na and the Gabarus Bay super port in my riding as the site of a possible new and very large steel complex in eastern Canada.
Later, after the question period, it was brought to my attention that approximately 27 bus loads of Quebec citizens were engaging in a peaceful demonstration in front of the House of Commons to show their support for the involvement of the federal government in the development of their super port. The people of Cape Breton, and of Nova Scotia in general, are fearful that we will once again lose out in competition with the larger provinces of Canada in trying to attract such an industrial complex.
I had a meeting with three representatives of the Gros Cacouna delegation for one half hour, and they assured me that what they were looking for primarily was dry bulk transportation facilities to transport wheat, paper, etc., and that they wanted a grain elevator built there. They informed me that they were not now interested in the proposed large steel complex as such. Well, I have to take them at their word. There are some 36,000 people within a radius of 25 to 30 miles of Gros Cacouna, and since they have a high unemployment rate in that area of the Gaspe, I can understand their concern.
My worry is the some 130,000 people who live in the county of Cape Breton and who, to a major extent, depend upon either the complete renovation of the Sydney steel plant at the present site, or a new major complex at Gabarus Bay, which is a magnificent superport some 26 miles from the Sydney area. In order to make the Gabarus possibilities become a reality, a consortium of steel buyers has to be put together by the new Canstel Corporation recently set up by the Nova Scotia government.
When he appeared before the Standing Committee on Regional Economic Expansion, the minister, on May 6, 1975, said:
Two provinces, Nova Scotia and Quebec, have indicated a very real interest in having a major steel complex. Newfoundland is in the picture still but-I think this is fair and I believe I saw where Premier Moores was quoted recently on this-they are not as far along the line as the others are.
The minister went on to say:
I am by no means convinced that it is a mutually exclusive proposition, in so far as, let us say, Quebec and Nova Scotia are concerned ... I think it is quite possible... to satisfy both provinces and indeed perhaps to have additional benefits for other provinces out of this kind of undertaking.
On that occasion the minister guaranteed to me that nothing would be done that would in any sense jeopardize the Sysco type of operation. I quote him again as follows: That is to jeopardize the existing jobs or to in some way or other act in a manner that would be detrimental to the future of the Sysco company and its employees.
We in Nova Scotia are glad to have the DREE minister put that statement on behalf of the Government of Canada publicly on the record. However, I want to make two comments on this matter in the short period at my disposal this evening.
Adjournment Debate
First, I think that the failure of the federal government of Canada to make the Cape Breton Development Corporation, which it set up in 1967, responsible also for the development of the Sydney Steel industry was an error of major magnitude-and this is not hindsight on my part for I said so publicly at the time. The result was that a relatively small province with inadequate finances, and little or no bureaucratic civil service expertise on international steel matters, was practically forced to fend for itself without adequate support or leadership from the federal government and its agency, the Cape Breton Development Corporation, even though the latter did indirectly subsidize the Sydney Steel Corporation in the late sixties and early seventies with low prices for coking coal.
It is true also that DREE made intermittent grants to Sysco, but the judgment is still valid that they did not play anywhere near the leadership or support role that they ought to have played. We are suffering to this day for that. As a member of parliament from that area-in fact one of the reasons for my entering into politics was of that failure-I feel that they have a special obligation to the people of that area and to Nova Scotia on this whole question of a future site location for a major steel complex.
Second, while economic factors have to play a most important role in such site location decisions, the political power of the province of Quebec in the federal Liberal caucus and otherwise, should not be a major element to be used against Nova Scotia in its legitimate quest to become a "have" province within the context of this Canadian confederation.

speakeroldname: Mr. Joseph-Philippe Guay (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Regional Economic Expansion):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion; Whip of the Liberal Party
subtopic: TRANSPORT-REQUEST FOR ASSURANCE PROPOSED PORT OF GROS CACOUNA WILL NOT SUPPLANT GABARUS BAY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the hon. member is aware, the project at Gros Cacouna is under serious consideration by officials at MOT. The Quebec government has approved the project in principle.
The Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) has discussed this project with Quebec provincial officials. Talks between MOT and provincial officials are presently under way. They are studying such things as the complementary aspect of this project vis-a-vis other Canadian ports. As the hon. member is aware, the Scott report, presently before Cabinet, deals with this very important issue of port development in Canada.
I am reminding the hon. member that the minister responsible for regional economic expansion tabled a preliminary report on a study commissioned by his ministry on November 26, 1974. In it it was determined that six deep water facilities, including Gabarus Bay and Gros Cacouna, were considered to have potential for development of a steel complex.
I should like to emphasize to the hon. member that it is the responsibility of the provinces to develop viable proposals. Essentially, the provinces will be competing among themselves with respect to the possibility of a steel complex being built. Owing to the magnitude of such an interprise it is obvious that the federal government will be very interested in proposals brought forward.
